docs.title: Introduction
docs.text:
Soundtracks are always important for any piece of media, whether it be movies, television, stage productions, or even video games. When we use music to complement media, it can enhance and deepen meaning within them. We believe that this is especially poignant within story, and that soundtracks use unique and important techniques to add meaning to stories, building them and shaping them with auditory landscapes.

In this User Guide we'll analyze a few cases where soundtracks have been particularly influential to a certain piece of media. By selecting one musical technique and tracing how a certain soundtrack uses it—and also how it's successful—we hope to show how these techniques are used in practice, and how other creators might be able to use them too. Listed below are our case studies and chosen topics.

  • KPOP Demon Hunters: How Cultural References Deepen Thematic Messages; By Alexander M.
  • Deltarune: How Developing Themes and Leitmotifs Complements Actions and Consequences; By Chase W.
  • Stardew Valley: How Music Affects Atmosphere; By Mira C.

docs.title: KPOP DEMON HUNTERS Soundtrack
docs.text: Written by Alexander Matthews

docs.title: Cultural Context and References in Music
Music - A Universal Language?
docs.text:
Is music a universal language? With the landmark success of Netflix's most-streamed movie ever, KPOP DEMON HUNTERS, it might certainly seem so.

The movie's breakout song Golden, by starring girl group HUNTR/X, spent 8 weeks at No. 1 on the Billboard Top 100, then another 8 weeks at No. 2. HUNTR/X's demon boy band rivals, the Saja Boys, have had similar success; their song Your Idol outperformed BTS to reach No. 2 on Spotify in the US, a historic high for a KPop boy band. The soundtrack album was the second most streamed album worldwide on Spotify for 2025.

And yet, even as beloved as the music of the movie is, there's a lot of cultural context in it that casual audiences missed.

docs.title: The Soundtrack Album: Cultural Context for Non-Korean Audiences
docs.text:
Track Title 1 TAKEDOWN (by TWICE) 2 How It's Done 3 Soda Pop 4 Golden 5 Strategy (by TWICE) 6 Takedown 7 Your Idol 8 Free 9 What It Sounds Like 10 사랑인가 봐 Love, Maybe (by MeloMance) 11 오솔길 Path (by Jokers) 12 Score Suite

Many of the underlying themes in the soundtrack require some familiarity with Korean culture to catch. If KPOP DEMON HUNTERS was your introduction to Korean media, understanding the cultural context behind the songs will help you understand their full meaning in the story!

docs.title: The Sound of K-Dramas
docs.text:
For instance, take protagonist Rumi, the leader and center of HUNTR/X and her eventual love interest and sympathetic antagonist Jinu, leader and center of the Saja Boys.

KPop Terminology

The "leader" of a KPop group is in charge of supervising other members and communicating with management, as well as representing the group during public activities like award festivals. The "center" of a KPop group is the member who's most often highlighted in songs and promotional material. This position often changes with time, even when group members remain the same.

"Love, Maybe," which plays when HUNTR/X first see the Saja Boys, is from the popular Korean drama Business Proposal, which brings immediate emotional context to the scene. When Jinu bumps Rumi's shoulder, sending her falling in slow motion toward the ground, audience members familiar with K-Dramas are left on tenterhooks, waiting for him to sweep in and save her like a total heartthrob. Thus, when Jinu instead lets her crash to the ground with a parting insult, the audience's negative impression of him is amplified.

docs.title: Idol-Fan Relationships
docs.text:
KPop has a massive amount of surrounding cultural context, and nowhere is this more crucial to understanding the story than for the song Your Idol, by the Saja Boys. The lyrics are a clear double entendre, speaking about absorbing fans' love and energy; the Saja Boys are demons attempting to steal their fans' souls, and it might seem odd to some audience members that they're not attempting to hide that. But, for KPop fans, Your Idol doesn't appear to be about demons at all. Instead, it comes off as a poignant commentary on the idol industry and negative idol-fan relationships.

KPop fans are famously devoted to their favourite groups and their bias, but this can lead to dependency and parasocial relationships, as well as hostility between fans or between fans and outsiders.

KPop Terminology

A fan's "bias" refers to their favourite member of a group, and some fans are strictly loyal only to that single member.

Songwriter EJAE, also the singing voice of Rumi and composer of many of the movie's songs, explained in an interview that Your Idol was largely inspired by her own experience as a KPop trainee. Despite trainees having not debuted as artists, fans would wait outside their training building until late at night. Some interacted with the trainees positively, requesting autographs, while others verbally insulted and abused the trainees. She wrote Your Idol to reflect two harmful relationships: that of demons consuming the souls of their victims, and that of KPop groups building a parasocial dependency in their fans.

docs.title: Using Context as an Audience Member
docs.text: Now that you know the cultural context behind some of the music, think of how it changes your understanding of the characters next time you watch the movie. How do Rumi and HUNTR/X feel when fighting the Saja Boys after hearing Your Idol, a song about KPOP groups unashamedly taking advantage of fans? How do you think HUNTR/X cultivate a healthier relationship with their fans? There's a lot of new information to find, if you only listen for it!

docs.title: Deltarune
docs.text: Written by Chase Wootton

docs.title: Toby Fox, Deltarune, and Leitmotifs
docs.text: Toby Fox—creator of Undertale and Deltarune—is notorious for intricately using leitmotifs: musical technique where a composer establishes a melody associated with a character, theme, or circumstance, then reuses that melody in other places in a collection of music. They are all over his music, and Deltarune—his most recent work—is a perfect example of how they can be interpreted to gain deeper meaning of a piece media's plot of themes. In Deltarune's soundtrack, Fox uses leitmotifs to reveal new things about characters, foreshadow how plot points are related, or create a specific tone and/or atmosphere, strengthening Deltarune's prophecy- and mystery-based narrative. In this page, then, we'll focus on one instance of leitmotif use, the Sanctuaries of Chapter 4, to see how Toby Fox uses this technique effectively, understanding how it can connect to narrative and story.

docs.title: The Sanctuaries
docs.text: "The Sanctuaries" refers to three distinct fantasy worlds—or "Dark Worlds"—that the player and their companions visit while the story progresses. Specifically, the moniker "Sanctuary" comes from the names of the musical tracks that play as the background music while the player is in these areas. These tracks are named "Dark Sanctuary," "The Second Sanctuary," and "The Third Sanctuary."

docs.title: Dark Sanctuary
docs.text:
Maybe one of the first things you notice when you hear "Dark Sanctuary" is its 6/8 time signature1. All of the sanctuary songs focus on the eighth note, thought they progressively get more complex. Initially, the song uses a simple arpeggiated rhythm to support a main melody, which is layered with leitmotifs. Two motifs—"Don't Forget" and "The Legend"—make up the majority of the melody. "Don't Forget"—Deltarune's main theme—grounds the track in heroic tension and "The Legend" connects the song to the mysterious prophecy stated at the beginning of the game when that track plays. "Dark Sanctuary" mostly remixes these two songs, and its only unique leitmotif is the background arpeggio, which is expanded on later.

What we can take from this opening track, then, is that this area is meant to be one where Deltarune's "prophecy" is at the forefront of the player's mind, and excerpts are the prophecy are scattered throughout the area. This portion of the game marks Deltarune's midpoint, and the atmosphere is tense and climactic. This is the story's turning point.

docs.title: The Second Sanctuary
docs.text:
Here's where things get interesting.

"The Second Sanctuary" is shocking because it plays when one of the characters in the player's party—Susie—opens a second Dark World. Dark Worlds are considered dangerous, and a magic that is largely associated with villains. Susie's decision to open a second one, therefore, is meant to be foreboding and eerie.

"The Second Sanctuary" opens with a similar arpeggio as the first—an echo that resembles the first track. There is added space between echoes, and strings crescendos in the background, increasing tension. Then, the track reveals its true colors. The previous leitmotifs are heard again, but recontextualized for the story's tone and themes. Fox adapts the melody to slide along the musical throughline, using odd synths to slowly drag one pitch to the next without a break in-between.

Yet the most interesting part of this track is its time signatures (yes, plural!). The opening arpeggio is so disorienting because it is in 9/42—one past the typical expected beat. But after the intro, the time signature switches to 3/43. Finally, a 10/84 section appears, completely changing the feel of the song.

Through experimenting with the tone and organization of leitmotifs, then, and adding slightly adjusted meters, Toby Fox once again reiterates the themes present within the Sanctuaries. The player continues their prophetic journey, but Susie's influence on the new environment is tangible and wrong in a sense, distorting the music (and atmosphere) with her naive creation.

docs.title: The Third Sanctuary
docs.text:
"The Third Sanctuary" is at the Climax of Deltarune Chapter 4. After closing Susie's fountain, the party must descend even deeper into the third Dark World of this Chapter. Not only does this indicate a descent into more secrets, more reveals relating to the prophecy, and a final confrontation with this chapter's villain—the Roaring Knight—but it continues to develop the leitmotifs that have been used throughout this chapter so far, and it continues the theme of the Dark Fountains' entropic nature, that will eventually culminate in the Roaring Knight making yet another fountain inside of a Dark World, creating a monster prophesied to bring the world closer to catastrophe.

"The Third Sanctuary" is very similar in structure to "The Second Sanctuary." It retains the arpeggiated 9/4 opening, the 10/8 sequence, and development of the same themes, but each technique used thus far is intensified and augmented to reflect theme and atmosphere.

The differences are prevalent, when you look at them. The Third Sanctuary relies heavily on arpeggiated 8th notes, which now comprise the main melody of the song. Additionally, the "The Legend" melody is heard only once (and quietly) while the "Don't Forget" leitmotif is discarded entirely. The removal of the "Don't Forget" leitmotif is particularly shocking, suggesting distance from its suggestion that "I'm with you in the dark."

But once again, time signature are by far the most prevalent difference. The Third Sanctuary is famous for its odd and sometimes baffling time signatures, and represents the culmination of the Sanctuaries' development. The main melody is in 11/85, one less than a clean 3 or 4 beat organization. This—and a rapid drum beat—provide energy to the track that drives it forward; one measure "falls" into the next. Additionally, at one point a 2/4 beat is added arbitrarily, and the song's conclusion is in a mind-boggling 23/86. Each movement creates tension and forward motion, as the environment becomes more and more alien. It's building to a conclusion, and it leads beautifully into this Chapter's climax.

docs.title: Conclusion
docs.text:
Through repetitive musical themes (leitmotifs), developing melodies, entropic organizations, and odd time signatures, Toby Fox creates a cascading motion throughout the Sanctuaries that culminates in the Third Sanctuary and the climax of Deltarune Chapter 4. He tells a story not only through plot but through atmosphere and tone conveyed through music. How these techniques are used in the Sanctuaries is an impressive case study on how leitmotifs can be changed and recontextualized to tell story that we can certainly learn from. Leitmotifs are a powerful tool, and Deltarune, Toby Fox, and the Sanctuary themes show how they can be used to create amazing effects that effortlessly complement the media they're in.

  1. That is, 6 eighth notes per measure. Most songs are in 4/4: 4 quarter notes per measure. ↩

  2. 9 quarter notes per measure. ↩

  3. This is different from 6/8 because the emphasis is placed on each quarter note, rather than each group of three eighth notes. ↩

  4. 10 eighth notes per measure. This could also reasonably counted as 5/4 ↩

  5. 11 eighth notes per measure! ↩

  6. A whopping 23 eighth notes per measure; usually counted as a section of 12/8 then a section of 11/8. ↩

docs.title: Stardew Valley
docs.text: Written by Mary 'Mira' Conner

docs.title: About the Music
docs.text:
The Stardew Valley Official Soundtrack is composed by ConcernedApe, the game's creator.

The original soundtrack featured 70 songs. Since then, the following have been added with each update:

  • Four songs from v1.1 in November 2017
  • Three songs from v1.3 in August 2018
  • Fourteen songs from v1.4 in November 2019
  • Nine songs from v1.5 in December 2020

Info

For a full list of tracks included in the game, visit the Stardew Valley Wiki.

docs.title: Triggering the Tunes
docs.text:
Each of the 100 songs currently featured in Stardew Valley features a set of specific conditions in which the song can be triggered. For example, "Summit Celebration" can only be heard when entering the finale cutscene of the game. Other songs can be heard multiple places, times, or even on command using a Mini-Jukebox.

When and why a song is triggered is an important aspect of the Stardew Valley's atmosphere. Atmosphere is defined as the sensory "feeling" that is evoked through visuals, audio, storytelling, and gameplay mechanics.

docs.title: Sounds of the Season
docs.text: There are twelve total seasonal tracks, three for each of the four seasons. At the beginning of each day, a single track is selected to play, and it will not loop once it has concluded. However, if no music is playing, the song will begin again upon entering any seasonal-track area.

docs.title: Character Themes
docs.text:
Of the 45 characters in Stardew Valley, 14 have songs named after them.

Character Song Title Grandpa Grandpa's Theme Wizard A Glimpse of the Other World Penny Pleasant Memory Elliott Piano Solo Leah Land of Green and Gold Abigail A Stillness in the Rain Maru Starwatcher Alex A Sad Song Haley Pickle Jar Rag Sebastian Echos Dr. Harvey Grapefruit Sky Shane Frozen Pizza and Eggs Emily Song of Feathers Leo Leo's Song

Character themes (sometimes labeled as melodies in the official soundtrack) are often played during deeply impactful moments involving a specific NPC.

docs.title: The Sound of Silence
docs.text:
The following locations are always silent

  • Basement Room of the Wizard
  • Beach
  • Blacksmith
  • Casino
  • Elliott's Cabin
  • Fish Shop and its back room
  • Jungle
  • JojaMart
  • Mutant Bug Lair
  • Pirate Cove (when empty)
  • Qi's Walnut Room
  • Quarry Mine
  • Sewers
  • Skull Cavern entrance
  • Spa
  • Tunnel
  • Witch's Hut
  • Witch's Swamp.

Sometimes, silence itself can be more impactful than any music. Certain locations are always silent, while others are silent only other certain conditions.

The Railroad is silent except during Winter. Outside areas and most stores are silent during Rain.png Rain and Thunderstorm.png Storm days. If a non-seasonal-track is playing, and the player enters a seasonal-track area (Town apart), there will be silence (e.g., entering the Forest from Town when the Town theme is playing, exiting the Adventurer's Guild, the Secret Woods, the Wizard's Tower...). Exiting Treehouse makes exception to the rule: the track playing before the entering plays.
